content: Artemisinin derivatives are considered advantageous over quinoline drugs for the treatment of severe malaria due to their rapid action and efficacy against malaria parasites that are resistant to quinine. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of artemisinin-based drugs in managing severe and complicated falciparum malaria in both adults and children. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Science Citation Index, LILACS, and African Index Medicus. Additionally, conference abstracts and reference lists of relevant articles were examined. Researchers, organizations, and pharmaceutical companies were also contacted to gather further information. The review included randomized and pseudo-randomized trials that compared artemisinin drugs (administered rectally, intramuscularly, or intravenously) with standard treatments, as well as comparisons between different artemisinin derivatives in patients with severe or complicated falciparum malaria. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, evaluated trial quality, and extracted data. Study authors were contacted when additional information was required. A total of 23 trials were included in the review. Among these, allocation concealment was deemed adequate in nine trials. Sixteen trials compared artemisinin drugs with quinine, involving a total of 2,653 patients. The use of artemisinin drugs was associated with improved survival rates, with a mortality odds ratio of 0.61 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.46 to 0.82) based on a random-effects model. However, in the subset of trials with adequate allocation concealment (2,261 patients), the survival benefit was only marginally statistically significant, with an odds ratio of 0.72 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.96). In a subgroup of 1,939 patients with cerebral malaria, the overall mortality was lower in those treated with artemisinin drugs, with an odds ratio of 0.63 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.88). However, when only trials with adequate allocation concealment were analyzed (1,607 patients), the difference in mortality was not statistically significant, with an odds ratio of 0.78 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.10). No significant differences were observed in the incidence of neurological sequelae between the treatment groups. Artemisinin drugs demonstrated faster clearance of malaria parasites from the bloodstream compared to quinine, and the adverse effects associated with both treatments were similar. The authors concluded that artemisinin drugs are at least as effective as quinine in preventing death in cases of severe or complicated malaria. No single artemisinin derivative appeared to be superior to the others. It is important to note that this review summarizes trials conducted up to 1999, and the authors have decided not to update this review further for reasons outlined in the What's new section.
